title: The Unknown Woman ("La Sconosciuta")
full_review:
The latest film from the director of "Cinema Paradiso" has won several prestigious European film awards, including five David di Donatello Awards (the Italian Oscar), best film among them -- with that last honor also bestowed by the Italian film critics. The film also was the Italian entry for this year's Academy Awards.

Unarguably well crafted, "The Unknown Woman" ("La Sconosciuta") (Outsider) proves an intriguing though often sordid mystery story centering on troubled Ukrainian immigrant Irena (played by Russian actress Xenia Rappoport in a fine, multifaceted performance) desperately seeking employment in an Italian town.

Haunted by her past sexual enslavement to a brutish pimp named Mold (Michele Placido) -- relived in numerous brief but horrifying flashbacks -- she contrives to become the housekeeper to wealthy jewelers Valeria and Donato Adacher (Claudia Gerini and Pierfrancesco Favino), and their troubled child Thea (Clara Dossena).

Director and co-writer Giuseppe Tornatore's melodrama is stylish, suspenseful and well acted. For a while, it's difficult to empathize with Irena, as we don't understand the motives behind her devious -- not to mention downright criminal -- actions, including getting the Adachers' longtime maid out of the way by sending her rolling down scores of steps on a deadly spiral staircase.

The plot is largely improbable and at times predictable. And that includes the sentimental and redemptive plot resolution for its morally ambiguous heroine.

The flashback sequences, besides illustrating Irena's idyllic romance with a handsome young man, also contain scenes of disturbing depravity and will be a turnoff for many, even as they illustrate today's widespread sex-trafficking epidemic.

Italian. English subtitles.

The film contains sporadic violence, including attempted murder with bloodshed; brief sexual encounters, some aberrant; torture; full female and rear-male nudity; a few rough and crude expletives; and one profanity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. Not rated by the Motion Picture Association of America.
